Stockpiling as a reserve fund is not the reason the text gives (wrong_detail). Distributing to the poor sounds reasonable but is not mentioned here (true_but_off). Submitting as tribute is the opposite of the decree's intent, which provides supplies rather than reclaims them (wrong_detail).

content: According to Ezra 6, at the dedication of the temple, the people offered twelve male goats as a sin offering to symbolize what?
options: The twelve elders who returned from exile
The twelve tribes of Israel
The twelve months of a sacred year
The twelve cities allotted to the Levites
explanation: Ezra 6:17 records that they offered 'twelve male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, as a sin offering for all Israel.' The twelve elders who returned from exile is not the meaning the text assigns to this number (wrong_detail). The twelve months of a sacred year is a misinterpretation not found in the context (common_misconception). The twelve Levitical cities is a detail belonging to the land allocation laws, unrelated to this offering (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra 6, after the dedication of the temple, according to what pattern did the people organize the priests and Levites to serve God in Jerusalem?
options: According to the ordinances of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah
According to the decree of King Darius
As it is written in the Book of Moses
According to the divisions David had established in former times
explanation: Ezra 6:18 records that they 'set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.' The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the construction but were not the pattern for the priestly divisions here (true_but_off). Darius's decree concerned the costs and protection of the project, not the assignment of priestly divisions (wrong_detail). David's divisions are a genuine tradition, but this verse attributes the pattern to the Book of Moses, not to David (common_misconception).

content: According to Ezra 6, which of the following was something Darius ADDED ON HIS OWN to his decree, and was NOT part of the original edict of Cyrus that had been found?
options: The order commanding Tattenai and his associates to stay away and let the work proceed
Permission for the people to rebuild the temple on its original site in Jerusalem
The specification that the height and width of the temple were each to be sixty cubits
The instruction to return the gold and silver vessels to the temple
explanation: The original edict of Cyrus (6:3–5) included: permission to rebuild the temple on its original site, the dimensions of sixty cubits, and the return of the gold and silver vessels. What Darius added begins in 6:6, commanding Tattenai and his colleagues in the province Beyond the River to 'keep away from there' so the work would not be hindered. Thus the correct answer is the order for Tattenai to stay away. Permission to rebuild on the original site belongs to Cyrus's edict (near_passage). The sixty-cubit dimensions belong to Cyrus's edict (near_passage). The return of the gold and silver vessels also belongs to Cyrus's edict (near_passage). This question requires distinguishing the boundary between two decrees within the same chapter.

content: According to Ezra 6, why were the returned exiles able to celebrate the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, even though they had previously faced opposition and interruptions to the construction?
options: Because the LORD had turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them, so as to strengthen their hands
Because the prophets Haggai and Zechariah had stood as guarantors before King Darius
Because the enemies around them had been punished and expelled from the land by King Darius
Because the number of returning exiles had grown as large as in the days before the captivity
explanation: Ezra 6:22 records that they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy 'for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God.' The prophets Haggai and Zechariah did support the construction (6:14), but the verse attributes the reason for joy to the LORD moving the king's heart, not to them acting as guarantors (true_but_off). The enemies being punished and expelled from the land is not mentioned in the text as the reason (wrong_detail). The number of returning exiles growing is not the stated reason in this verse (wrong_scope). This question requires tracing the theological cause the text emphasizes rather than secondary factors.

content: According to the genealogy at the opening of Ezra chapter 7, to which high priest is Ezra's lineage ultimately traced back?
options: Aaron
Melchizedek
Zadok
Eli
explanation: Ezra 7:1-5 traces Ezra's genealogy through many generations back to 'Aaron the chief priest.' (B) Melchizedek was a priest in Abraham's time but does not belong to this genealogy (wrong_scope). (C) Zadok appears within this lineage but is not the ultimate source (near_passage). (D) Eli was a priest in Samuel's time and does not appear in this genealogy (wrong_detail).

content: According to Ezra chapter 7, in which year of King Artaxerxes' reign did Ezra and the company returning to Jerusalem set out?
options: The seventh year
The first year
The twentieth year
The thirty-second year
explanation: Ezra 7:7 records that some of the people went up to Jerusalem 'in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes.' (B) The first year was when Cyrus issued his decree in chapter 1, not this return (near_passage). (C) The twentieth year was when Nehemiah was sent, which belongs to a different book (wrong_scope). (D) The thirty-second year is associated with Nehemiah's later return, not Ezra's (wrong_scope).

content: According to the king's decree in Ezra chapter 7, what privilege were temple servants such as priests and Levites granted?
options: Exemption from tax, tribute, and toll
A salary paid from the royal treasury
A grant of farmland surrounding the temple
The right to command the provincial army
explanation: Ezra 7:24 forbids imposing 'tax, tribute, or toll' on the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, and temple servants. (B) The king provided silver and gold for the temple but did not establish a monthly salary for them (wrong_detail). (C) Any grant of farmland is not mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). (D) They served in the temple and had no connection to commanding the army (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra chapter 7, upon perceiving what upon himself did Ezra take courage to gather the leading men to go up with him?
options: The hand of the LORD his God was upon him
The protection of the royal army
The pledge of the king's seven counselors
The abundant wealth in the king's treasury
explanation: Ezra 7:28 records that he took courage 'for the hand of the LORD my God was upon me.' (B) Later Ezra was even ashamed to ask the king for a military escort (Ezra 8:22), so royal protection was not his source of courage (true_but_off). (C) The seven counselors had a part in the commission (v. 14) but were not what gave him confidence (near_passage). (D) The treasury wealth is mentioned in the decree but was not the reason for his courage (true_but_off).

content: In the opening of King Artaxerxes' letter in Ezra chapter 7, by what title does the king style himself when writing to Ezra?
options: King of kings
King of all the earth
King chosen by Heaven
King over all peoples
explanation: Ezra 7:12 opens: 'Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest...' (B) 'King of all the earth' echoes how Cyrus styled himself in the decree of chapter 1, not this letter (near_passage). (C) The phrase 'chosen by Heaven' does not appear in the text, even though the king acknowledges the God of heaven (wrong_detail). (D) 'King over all peoples' is a mistaken restatement of a detail from the actual title (wrong_detail).

content: According to the letter in Ezra chapter 7, what mission did the king assign to Ezra when sending him back to Judah and Jerusalem?
options: To inquire about Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of his God
To rebuild the broken-down walls of Jerusalem
To collect taxes for the royal treasury throughout the region beyond the River
To appoint Ezra as governor to rule over all the land of Judah
explanation: Ezra 7:14 states that the king and his seven counselors sent him to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of his God. (B) Rebuilding the walls was the mission of Nehemiah, not Ezra (wrong_scope). (C) On the contrary, the decree even exempted temple servants from taxes (v.24), so collecting taxes is incorrect (wrong_detail). (D) The king gave him authority to appoint judges (v.25) but did not appoint him as governor (wrong_detail).

content: In the decree supplying goods for the temple in Ezra chapter 7, what item were the treasurers ordered to provide without any limit on quantity?
options: Salt
Wheat
Wine
Oil
explanation: Ezra 7:22 sets maximum limits for silver, wheat, wine, and oil, but specifies 'salt without prescribing how much.' (B) Wheat was limited to one hundred cors, so it is not the answer (wrong_detail). (C) Wine also had a limit of one hundred baths (wrong_detail). (D) Oil was likewise limited to one hundred baths, unlike salt which was provided without restriction (wrong_detail).

content: According to the reason the king gave in Ezra chapter 7, why must everything commanded by God be diligently carried out for the temple?
options: Lest wrath come upon the realm of the king and his sons
Lest the people of Judah revolt against the royal court
So that God would grant the king a long life
So that the king's fame would be remembered forever
explanation: Ezra 7:23 states the reason: 'lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons.' (B) The text does not mention any risk of the people revolting (wrong_detail). (C) 'A long life' is a different motivation not mentioned in the decree at this point (wrong_detail). (D) While the king did seek blessing, this verse emphasizes avoiding God's wrath rather than securing lasting fame (true_but_off).

content: According to the end of the decree in Ezra chapter 7, what authority did the king grant Ezra, and on what dual legal basis was judgment to be rendered?
options: To appoint magistrates and judges, according to both the law of his God and the law of the king
To appoint magistrates and judges, according to the law of his God alone
To personally adjudicate all cases, according to both the law of his God and the law of the king
To appoint magistrates and judges, according to both the law of Moses and Persian custom
explanation: Ezra 7:25-26 grants Ezra authority to appoint 'magistrates and judges' to judge the people, while v.26 requires that anyone who does not obey 'the law of your God and the law of the king' be punished. (B) Almost right: correct on appointing judges, but omits 'the law of the king,' whereas v.26 names both (wrong_detail). (C) Almost right: correctly identifies the dual legal basis, but wrong in that Ezra was tasked with appointing judges rather than personally adjudicating every case (wrong_detail). (D) While 'the law of the king' does refer to Persian law, the text calls it 'the law of the king' not 'Persian custom,' and the paired standard is 'the law of your God' rather than specifically 'the law of Moses' (true_but_off).

content: Based on the dates recorded in Ezra chapter 7, when did the group depart and when did they arrive in Jerusalem, both within the same year?
options: Departed on the first day of the first month, arrived on the first day of the fifth month
Departed on the first day of the first month, arrived in the seventh month
Departed in the fifth month, arrived in the seventh month
Departed on the first day of the first month, arrived on the tenth day of the fifth month
explanation: Ezra 7:9 records that 'on the first day of the first month the journey up from Babylon was begun, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem'; v.8 confirms arrival in the fifth month. (B) Almost right: correct on the departure date but changes the arrival month from the fifth to the seventh (wrong_detail). (C) Wrong on both the departure and arrival dates, confusing them with other months associated with the king's reign (wrong_detail). (D) Almost right: correct that arrival was in the fifth month, but the text says 'the first day,' not 'the tenth' (wrong_detail).

content: When Ezra gathered the people by the river that runs to Ahava and reviewed them, he found that no one from which group was present, prompting him to send for more?
options: The Levites
The priests
The Nethinim
The singers
explanation: Ezra 8:15 records that he reviewed the people and the priests but found 'none of the sons of Levi there,' so he sent messengers to seek servants for the house of God. The priests (wrong_detail) were in fact already present; it was precisely because they were there that the absence of the Levites became apparent. The Nethinim (near_passage) are mentioned in v.20 but they joined the group rather than being the missing ones. The singers (wrong_scope) are not the group identified as absent in this passage.

content: What was the primary purpose of the fast that Ezra proclaimed by the Ahava River?
options: To humble themselves and seek from God a safe journey
To mourn over the sins that their ancestors had committed against God
To repent because the people had married foreign women in violation of the law
To give thanks because the group had arrived in Jerusalem safely
explanation: Ezra 8:21 records that he proclaimed a fast 'that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods.' Mourning over ancestral sins (wrong_scope) is a theme in other chapters, not the purpose of this passage. Repentance for intermarriage (wrong_scope) belongs to Ezra 9–10, after the journey. Giving thanks for arriving safely (wrong_detail) is incorrect because the fast took place before the group set out, not after they arrived.

content: How many leading priests did Ezra set apart to be entrusted with the silver, gold, and vessels offered for the temple?
options: Twelve men
Seven men
Ten men
Twenty-four men
explanation: Ezra 8:24 records that he 'set apart twelve of the leading priests' to weigh and hand over the offerings. Seven men (wrong_detail) is a number associated with other forms of organization (such as deacons) but not here. Ten men (wrong_detail) is close in number but incorrect. Twenty-four men (common_misconception) refers to the twenty-four divisions of priests established in David's time, not the number set apart here.

content: On the journey to Jerusalem, how did the hand of God protect Ezra's group?
options: He delivered them from the hand of enemies and those who lay in ambush along the way
He sent favorable rains so they would have enough water to drink along the way
He caused the kings along the road to come out and receive them with great ceremony
He healed all those who were sick in the group along the way
explanation: Ezra 8:31 records, 'The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way.' Sending rain for water (wrong_detail) is not mentioned in this passage. Kings coming out to receive them (wrong_scope) does not appear in the journey narrative; the favor shown by the king took place in chapter 7. Healing the sick (wrong_detail) is not the form of protection described here.

content: Why did Ezra decide not to ask the king for soldiers and cavalry to protect the group on the journey?
options: Because he had told the king that the hand of God is on all who seek him
Because the king had flatly refused when Ezra made the request for an armed escort
Because the group was large enough and strong enough to defend itself along the way
Because the law forbade priests from relying on the soldiers of a foreign nation
explanation: Ezra 8:22 explains that he 'was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us... for we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him"'; to request an escort would have contradicted that testimony. The king refusing (wrong_detail) contradicts the text: Ezra proactively chose not to ask rather than being turned down. The group being strong enough to defend itself (wrong_scope) is not the reason given; in fact they fasted and prayed precisely because they knew they were vulnerable. The law forbidding reliance on foreign soldiers (common_misconception) is an inference beyond the text and is not the reason stated.

content: When entrusting the treasures to the twelve priests, what did Ezra emphasize about the priests and the vessels so they would be aware of their responsibility to guard them?
options: They are holy to the LORD, the vessels are also holy, and the silver and gold are a freewill offering
They must recount the silver and gold once every day regularly throughout the journey
They would be sentenced to death if any vessel was lost
They were permitted to use a portion of the silver to cover food expenses along the way
explanation: Ezra 8:28 records him saying, 'You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD.' Recounting daily (wrong_detail) is not mentioned; the weighing was done only at the time of entrusting and receiving (vv.33–34). Being sentenced to death (wrong_scope) is an inference beyond the text — no such threat appears. Using a portion of the silver for travel expenses (common_misconception) contradicts the 'holy' and 'offered to the LORD' character that Ezra emphasized.

content: After arriving in Jerusalem, how were the silver, gold, and vessels weighed and handed over to ensure full transparency?
options: Everything was weighed and the quantities and weights were recorded at the time of handover
Only the number of vessels was counted, without re-weighing the silver and gold
The treasures were handed directly to the high priest with no witnesses present
The handover was postponed until after the burnt offerings had been presented
explanation: Ezra 8:33–34 records that the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed in the house of God and handed to the priests, 'all counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded' at that time. Only counting vessels without weighing the silver and gold (wrong_detail) is incorrect because both the silver and gold were also weighed. Handing over directly with no witnesses (wrong_scope) contradicts the text, which clearly indicates multiple witnesses and written records. Postponing until after the burnt offerings (wrong_detail) reverses the sequence: vv.33–34 show the weighing took place first, while the burnt offerings were presented in v.35.

content: When the returned exiles offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, what symbolic significance is reflected in the number of sacrificial animals?
options: Twelve bulls and twelve male goats, representing the twelve tribes
Seven bulls and seven rams, corresponding to the seven days of the week
Each clan that returned with Ezra offered its own bull
The number of sacrifices equaled the number of Levites found at Casiphia
explanation: Ezra 8:35 records they offered 'twelve bulls for all Israel… twelve male goats for a sin offering,' with the number twelve symbolizing the whole twelve tribes. Seven animals corresponding to the days of the week (wrong_detail) is wrong both in number and in meaning. One animal per returning clan (wrong_scope) does not match the fixed number twelve in the text. The number of sacrifices equaling the number of Levites found (near_passage) confuses this with the search for Levites at Casiphia (v.17), which has no connection to the number of sacrificial animals.

content: Ezra sent messengers to Iddo at Casiphia to seek servants for the house of God. In what essential way does the outcome differ from the request for an armed escort (v.22)?
options: Both relied on God's hand: here God provided the Levites, while for the escort Ezra refused to ask in order to preserve his testimony
The search for Levites succeeded because the king issued an order, while the escort failed because the king changed his mind
Both endeavors failed, so the group set out with neither Levites nor an armed escort
The search for Levites was accomplished through fasting, while soldiers were sought through burnt offerings
Both the Levites and the armed escort were provided by Iddo at Casiphia
explanation: Ezra 8:18 records, 'by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion' among the Levites, along with his relatives (vv.18–19) and many Nethinim (v.20); while in v.22 Ezra deliberately chose not to request soldiers from the king so as not to contradict his testimony about God's protection. Comparing both passages reveals the same principle of relying on 'God's hand' — yet in one case God supplied servants, while in the other Ezra voluntarily declined an escort. 'Through the king's order' (wrong_detail) is incorrect: the Levites came by God's hand through Iddo, not by royal command. 'Both endeavors failed' (wrong_detail) is wrong because the search for Levites succeeded. 'Soldiers through burnt offerings' (wrong_scope) confuses this with the offerings in v.35 made after the group had already arrived. 'Iddo provided both the Levites and the soldiers' (wrong_detail) is wrong because Iddo was connected only to the Levites; there is no mention of him supplying soldiers.

content: The spiritual sequence Ezra demonstrated — fasting before setting out and then arriving safely — most clearly illustrates which principle of faith?
options: Trusting God does not exclude supplication: he fasted and prayed, then God answered, rather than waiting passively
True faith requires refusing all human assistance in every circumstance
Prayer is only necessary once all natural means have first been exhausted
Safe passage is guaranteed as a reward for presenting burnt offerings before departing
explanation: Ezra 8:21–23 shows him fasting 'to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves,' and 'he listened to our entreaty'; faith in God's protection is coupled with active supplication, not passive waiting. Reading all three verses together reveals the relationship between trust (v.22) and petition (vv.21, 23). 'Refusing all human assistance in every circumstance' (common_misconception) is an overgeneralization; Ezra declined soldiers in this specific situation because of his testimony, not as an absolute rule. 'Prayer only when all natural means are exhausted' (common_misconception) reverses the order: he prayed first and did not treat prayer as a last resort. 'Safe passage as a reward for burnt offerings before departing' (wrong_detail) is wrong in sequence — the burnt offerings were presented after arriving (v.35), not before setting out.

content: According to Ezra 9:1, who came to inform Ezra about the sinful condition of the people?
options: The officials
The priests
The prophets
The clan leaders
explanation: Ezra 9:1 records: 'The officials approached me and said: The people of Israel… have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands.' The correct answer is The officials. 'The priests' is incorrect because they were among the group accused of sinning, not those who came to report (wrong_detail). 'The prophets' do not appear in this scene (wrong_scope). 'The clan leaders' gathered later in chapter 10; they were not the ones bringing the report in 9:1 (near_passage).

content: According to Ezra 9:2, what kind of violation were the officials and leaders accused of being foremost in?
options: In this unfaithfulness
In this idolatry
In this plundering
In this deception
explanation: Ezra 9:2 records: 'the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost in this unfaithfulness.' The correct answer is unfaithfulness regarding intermarriage with foreign women. 'Idolatry' is the potential consequence Ezra feared, not the sin explicitly named in this verse (common_misconception). 'Plundering' has no relevance to the context (wrong_scope). 'Deception' is not part of the accusation made here (wrong_detail).

content: According to Ezra 9:3, after tearing his garment and pulling hair from his head and beard, what did Ezra do until the time of the evening offering?
options: Sat appalled in silence
Went proclaiming throughout the city
Immediately summoned the people
Went to find the priests
explanation: Ezra 9:3–4 records that Ezra 'sat appalled' until the time of the evening sacrifice. The correct answer is sat appalled in silence. 'Went proclaiming throughout the city' does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). 'Immediately summoned the people' happened later, after the prayer (near_passage). 'Went to find the priests' is not recorded anywhere in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra 9:4, who gathered around Ezra while he sat appalled?
options: Those who trembled at the words of God
The Levites who were on duty guarding the temple
Those who had recently returned from Babylon
Those who were offering the evening burnt offering that day
explanation: Ezra 9:4 records: 'Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel… gathered around me.' The correct answer is those who trembled at the words of God. 'Levites on guard duty at the temple' is not the group identified in this verse (wrong_detail). 'Those who had recently returned from Babylon' describes the returnees in general, not the specific criterion stated in verse 4 (wrong_scope). 'Those offering the evening burnt offering' confuses this with the detail about the time of the evening sacrifice mentioned in the same verse (near_passage).

content: According to Ezra 9:5, what posture and gesture did Ezra take when he began to pray at the time of the evening sacrifice?
options: Fell on his knees and spread out his hands to the LORD his God
Stood upright and looked up toward heaven
Prostrated himself completely face down on the ground
Knelt but bowed his face and did not dare spread out his hands
explanation: Ezra 9:5 records that he rose from his fasting 'and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God.' The correct answer combines both kneeling and spreading out the hands. 'Standing upright and looking up' describes the wrong posture, since the verse explicitly states he knelt (wrong_detail). 'Prostrating face completely to the ground' is close but the text emphasizes kneeling and spreading out the hands rather than lying face down (almost_right/wrong_detail). 'Kneeling but bowing his face without daring to spread out his hands' is correct about kneeling but directly contradicts the detail 'spread out my hands' (almost_right/wrong_detail).

content: According to Ezra 9:7, when confessing sin on behalf of the people, how did Ezra describe the consequences of their ancestors' sins that had continued to that day?
options: Handed over to the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, and to shame
God withdrew from the temple and scattered the tribes
They lost the promised land and were permanently forbidden from returning to Jerusalem
They were rebuked by prophets and repeatedly struck with plague
explanation: Ezra 9:7 states that because of their sins, 'we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame.' The correct answer accurately lists these consequences. 'God withdrew from the temple and scattered the tribes' confuses this with a different concept not stated in this verse (wrong_detail). 'Lost the promised land and permanently forbidden from returning' contradicts the context, since the people had just been allowed to return (common_misconception). 'Rebuked by prophets and repeatedly struck with plague' is almost right but verse 7 speaks of the sword and captivity, not plague (wrong_detail).

content: According to Ezra 9:8, what image did Ezra use to describe the grace God had given to the remnant of the people?
options: A peg in his holy place and light granted to their eyes
A lamp burning brightly in a place of darkness
A wall of protection around the holy city
A fresh spring of water in the wilderness
explanation: Ezra 9:8 states that God had granted them favor 'to give us a peg in his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes.' The correct answer uses the precise images of 'a peg' and 'eyes brightened.' 'A lamp burning brightly' sounds close to the idea of eyes being brightened but is not the image the text actually uses (wrong_detail). 'A wall of protection' is an image found in Nehemiah, not in this passage (near_passage). 'A fresh spring of water' does not appear in this verse at all (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra 9:9, although the people were servants, what did Ezra say God had moved the kings of Persia to do for them?
options: Granted them revival to rebuild the temple and a protective wall around them
Made them prosperous and exempted them from all tribute and taxes
Appointed a separate king to rule over them in Judah
Gave them authority to drive out the surrounding peoples
explanation: Ezra 9:9 states that God moved the kings of Persia to show them steadfast love, 'to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God… and to grant us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.' The correct answer accurately names the rebuilding of the temple and the protective wall. 'Made prosperous and exempted from taxes' is almost right but this verse concerns the revival of the temple, not tax exemption (wrong_detail). 'Appointed a separate king to rule in Judah' contradicts the reality that they remained under Persian authority (common_misconception). 'Authority to drive out the surrounding peoples' is not found in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra 9:11-12, what did Ezra recall that the prophets had commanded the people not to do with the peoples of the land, and for what long-term purposes?
options: Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, so that the people may be strong, eat the best of the land, and leave it as an inheritance to their children forever
Do not trade with them, so that the people may keep their wealth and pass the land on to their children
Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, so that the people may receive forgiveness and return home quickly
Do not learn their ways, so that the people may become powerful and establish an independent nation
explanation: Ezra 9:12 states: 'Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons… that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.' The correct answer includes both the prohibition on intermarriage and all three purposes (strength, eating the best of the land, leaving an inheritance). 'Do not trade… keep wealth' misrepresents the nature of the prohibition, changing intermarriage to commerce (wrong_detail). 'Do not give or take in marriage… to receive forgiveness and return home quickly' has the prohibition right but assigns the wrong purpose, since the verse speaks of strength and inheritance, not forgiveness (wrong_detail). 'Do not learn their ways… establish an independent nation' changes both the content of the prohibition and adds a purpose not found in the text (wrong_scope).

content: According to Ezra 9:13-15, what is the central argument in the closing section of Ezra's prayer before the righteous God?
options: God has punished them less than their sins deserved, so if they sin again, no one will be able to stand before him
Because God has punished them enough, the people have the right to ask him to fully forgive all remaining sins
Because the surrounding nations are more wicked, God must defend Israel as the innocent party
God established an everlasting covenant, so even if the people sin he is still obligated to preserve them
explanation: Ezra 9:13-15 states that God 'punished us less than our iniquities deserved,' then Ezra asks: if they again break his commandments by intermarrying with these abominable peoples, 'would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant?' and concludes: 'no one can stand before you.' The correct answer captures the logic: the punishment was already lighter than deserved, so no one can dare to sin again. 'God has punished enough so the people can demand full forgiveness' inverts the humble spirit of the prayer into a demand (common_misconception). 'The surrounding nations are more wicked so Israel is innocent' is the opposite of Ezra's intent, since he is confessing the guilt of his own people (wrong_detail). 'The everlasting covenant obligates God to preserve them despite sin' is almost right but verse 15 emphasizes that no one can stand before God, not that God is bound to tolerate sin (wrong_scope).

content: When Ezra prayed, confessed sin, and wept before the temple of God, what was the general attitude of the large crowd of Israelites gathered around him?
options: They wept bitterly with him
They quietly left and went home
They became angry and wanted to stone him
They rejoiced and sang praises
explanation: Ezra 10:1 records that the people gathered in 'a very great assembly, men, women, and children, and the people wept bitterly.' The option 'quietly left' contradicts the text's depiction of a large crowd gathering and weeping together (wrong_detail). 'Became angry and wanted to stone him' describes a hostile reaction not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Rejoiced and sang praises' is the opposite of the context of weeping and confession of sin (common_misconception).

content: In Ezra chapter 10, who was the first to speak up, acknowledging that the people had sinned against God while declaring there was still hope for Israel?
options: Shecaniah, son of Jehiel
Nehemiah, the cupbearer
Haggai, the prophet
Zerubbabel, the governor
explanation: Ezra 10:2 records: 'Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: We have broken faith with our God... but even now there is hope for Israel.' Nehemiah is a figure from the book of Nehemiah and does not appear here (wrong_scope). Haggai was a prophet active during the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5) but is not this speaker (near_passage). Zerubbabel led the first return of exiles but did not make this statement (near_passage).

content: Shecaniah proposed making a covenant with God. According to his words, what was the content of that covenant?
options: To send away all the foreign wives and the children born to them
To offer a sin offering for each family that had married a foreign wife
To forbid the people from entering the temple of God henceforth
To pay a tithe of their property to atone for wrongdoing against the foreigners
explanation: Ezra 10:3 records Shecaniah's proposal to 'make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God.' 'Offering a sin offering' is a plausible ritual solution but is not the content of the covenant stated here (true_but_off). 'Forbidding entry into the temple' runs contrary to the goal of restoring worship (wrong_detail). 'Paying a tithe' confuses the law of offerings with the act of repentance in this context (common_misconception).

content: After leaving the temple area, Ezra went into the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib and spent the night there. What act of abstinence showed that he was still grieving over the people's sin?
options: He ate no bread and drank no water
He did not sleep all day or night
He spoke not a word to anyone
He did not leave the room for seven days
explanation: Ezra 10:6 records that Ezra 'ate no bread and drank no water, for he was mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles.' 'Did not sleep all day or night' is another form of ascetic practice but is not what the text records (wrong_detail). 'Spoke not a word' recalls a vow of silence but is not found here (wrong_detail). 'Did not leave the room for seven days' imports a seven-day period from a different festival into this context (common_misconception).

content: The officials issued a proclamation summoning all the exiles to Jerusalem. According to the decree, what would happen to anyone who did not come within three days?
options: All their property would be forfeited and they would be banned from the assembly of the exiles
They would be fined one bull as a sin offering
They would be expelled from the land and exiled to Babylon again
They would be forbidden from participating in the Passover for an entire year
explanation: Ezra 10:8 records that anyone who did not come within three days, according to the command of the officials and elders, would have 'all his property forfeited, and he himself banned from the congregation of the exiles.' 'Fined one bull as a sin offering' is a plausible ritual penalty but is not what the text states (true_but_off). 'Expelled and exiled to Babylon again' is a severe consequence but is not recorded here (wrong_detail). 'Forbidden from the Passover for a year' confuses this with a penalty from a different law (common_misconception).

content: When all the people of Judah and Benjamin gathered at the square before the house of God within three days, besides their fear over the serious matter, what weather condition also made them tremble?
options: Because it was raining heavily
Because the sun was blazing hot
Because a sandstorm was blowing in
Because snow was covering the ground
explanation: Ezra 10:9 records that the people sat in the square 'trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain.' 'Blazing hot sun' contradicts the rain detail explicitly recorded in the text (wrong_detail). 'Sandstorm' is a different weather phenomenon not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Snow' is inappropriate and not recorded (common_misconception).

content: The people agreed to correct their wrongdoing, but what reason did they give for why the matter could not be resolved in a day or two?
options: The people were many, it was the rainy season, and those who had sinned were very numerous
Many of the foreign wives had already fled from the city
The officials had not yet agreed on the appropriate punishment
The temple was not yet finished, so there was no place to conduct proceedings
explanation: Ezra 10:13 records the people saying: 'the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open. Nor is this a task for one or two days, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter.' 'Foreign wives having fled' is a detail not present in the text (wrong_detail). 'Officials not yet agreeing on punishment' sounds plausible but is not the reason stated (true_but_off). 'Temple not yet finished' is wrong in context since the temple was completed back in chapter 6 (wrong_scope).

content: In the account of dealing with the matter of foreign marriages, certain individuals are named as taking a different position from the majority. What does verse 10:15 say about Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah?
options: They opposed the proposed plan for resolving the matter
They were appointed to lead the examination of each individual case
They were the first two to confess to having married foreign women
They refused to attend the assembly even after being summoned
explanation: Ezra 10:15 records: 'Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them' — meaning they opposed the proposed resolution plan. The option 'appointed to lead the examination' reverses their role: it was Ezra together with the heads of fathers' houses who sat to examine the cases (v. 16), so this is close but attributes the role to the wrong people (wrong_detail). 'The first two to confess to marrying foreign women' confuses them with the list of offenders at the end of the chapter (near_passage). 'Refusing to attend the assembly even after being summoned' confuses them with the penalty clause in v. 8 (common_misconception). The text must be read carefully to distinguish those who 'opposed the plan' from those who 'administered the examination.'

content: Ezra and the heads of fathers' houses sat to examine each case of foreign marriage. Comparing the start date and end date of the investigation, how long did the whole process take?
options: About three months, from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month
Exactly seven days, completing one full week
About six months, from the middle of the year to the end of the year
Exactly forty days, like the familiar period of fasting
explanation: Ezra 10:16 states they began to sit in examination 'on the first day of the tenth month,' while v. 17 records 'by the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women' — a span of about three months. 'Exactly seven days' confuses this with the duration of week-long festivals (common_misconception). 'About six months' misstates the time markers even though it uses a similar month-counting approach (wrong_detail). 'Forty days' borrows a familiar fasting figure but does not match the two time markers given in the text (common_misconception). This question requires reading and cross-referencing both time markers (vv. 16 and 17) to calculate the period.

content: The list of those who had married foreign women at the end of chapter 10 opens with which group?
options: Priests from the line of Jeshua
The gatekeepers of the temple
The singers in the house of God
Those who brought wood for the altar
explanation: Ezra 10:18 opens the list: 'Among the sons of the priests who had married foreign women were found: of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers...' and v. 19 records that they pledged to put away their wives. 'Gatekeepers' and 'singers' are indeed temple service groups that appear later in the list, not at its opening (near_passage). 'Those who brought wood for the altar' is a duty mentioned in Nehemiah, not the opening group of this list (wrong_scope).
